passages.nngroup: Contextual inquiry is a type of ethnographic field study in which researchers observe and interview a small number of users in their own environment while they work (Kim Flaherty, 6 Dec 2020). 4 grounding principles (context, partnership, interpretation, focus); 4-part session (primer, transition, contextual interview with a watch-then-discuss loop, wrap-up); master-apprentice model; sessions from 1 hour to several days; risks: interview mode, complaint session, researcher bias.
passages.wikipedia: Contextual inquiry is a user-centered design research method, part of the Contextual Design methodology (Holtzblatt and Beyer). One-on-one interview of about two hours; 4 users for a small task up to 30 or more; interpretation sessions with 3-8 team members; affinity diagram, work models, personas; reveals tacit knowledge; resource-intensive.
passages.dscout: A semi-structured interview that combines questions with observation in the participant's own environment; active inquiry vs passive inquiry; Hawthorne effect and social desirability bias; wrap-up to check interpretations (Nikki Anderson, 20 Jun 2023).
passages.luma: Interviewing and observing people in their own environment, approaching the work as an apprentice; benefits: real behavior, empathy, tests assumptions, credibility with stakeholders; 9-step quick guide incl. consent and recording.
passages.usertesting: A user-centered research method in which researchers watch and question people as they complete tasks in their everyday surroundings; 4 principles; 5-step process; observer bias; user behaviors vs self-reported behaviors; informed consent; remote observation as an alternative (Jennifer Henderson, 18 Apr 2024).
passages.thinkdesign: Participants are observed performing tasks and narrate what they do, leading the session more than in a standard interview; best for complex or enterprise systems and specialised work; disadvantages: time- and resource-intensive, interpretation, expectation management.
passages.nngroupVideo: Mayya Azarova (9 Sep 2022): 'how many users' has three parts, users per visit, visits per day and total visits, and the total depends on the project. No transcript on the page.

outline.answerHint: Contextual inquiry is a generative UX research method in which a researcher observes users doing real work in their own work setting and asks about each step as it happens. Karen Holtzblatt and Hugh Beyer developed it as the field step of Contextual Design.
points: Intro before this H2 (said-vs-did split, see variety): 2-3 sentences. The illustrative receiving clerk SAYS 'scan the pallet, confirm the count, done'; observation SHOWS a paper packing list, a second screen to look up the purchase order, a phone call to the buyer and a sticky note for the damaged carton. Keyword in the first sentence (carrier above). Then one sentence on what the post gives: the principles, a session plan, the questions, a field-note sheet and the path to design decisions.

UP link to the hub within the first 300 words, anchor exactly 'UX research services' (required by the orchestrator), e.g. 'contextual inquiry is one of the six deliverables in our UX research services'.

Definition paragraph: name the parent (generative research within UX research; expand 'user experience (UX)' once), the master-apprentice model (the user is the expert, the researcher learns like an apprentice), and Contextual Design (Holtzblatt and Beyer; fact-checker confirms the first-edition year 1997/1998 and that the 2nd edition 'Contextual Design: Design for Life' is 2016/2017; print only the confirmed year). Use the synonym 'field observation' once.

H3 'What does contextual mean in contextual inquiry?' (PAA cluster): everyday meaning first ('depending on the surrounding situation'), then the UX meaning: the contextual factors are the place, the tools and artifacts, the other people, the interruptions and the time pressure. One sentence: in UX, contextual analysis is the interpretation step covered in H2 9.
Answer 'what are contextual inquiries' implicitly (one session = one contextual inquiry; a study = several).

outline.h2: Why does contextual inquiry beat asking users what they do?
outline.answerHint: Contextual inquiry beats asking because observation in the real work setting captures what users do, while an interview captures what they remember and are willing to say. Experts automate steps they no longer notice (tacit knowledge), so they leave them out of any answer.
points: This is the owner's angle; make it the argument of the post, not a list of benefits. Three causes, each with one explanation: tacit knowledge (Wikipedia/Holtzblatt), recall gaps (people summarise a typical day, not the real one), social desirability bias (dscout) (people describe the correct procedure, not the workaround).
Visual 1: said-vs-did split card (see visuals), placed after the paragraph it explains; text version under it.

Counterpoint, honest: observation changes behavior too (Hawthorne effect; dscout lists tactics such as rapport and longer sessions). Explain why CI limits it: the user does their own work on their own deadline, so the task pulls them back to normal behavior. Label this reasoning as practitioner reasoning, no statistic.
Do NOT use the Margaret Mead quote LUMA prints ('What people say, what people do…'): the attribution is not verifiable. Do NOT reuse NN/g's auto-insurance autosave anecdote.

outline.h2: What are the four principles of contextual inquiry?
outline.answerHint: The four principles of contextual inquiry are context, partnership, interpretation and focus: observe users in the real work setting, share control of the session with them, check your interpretation with them on the spot, and steer every observation toward the research focus.
points: One H3 or table row per principle (children): what the researcher does, and the mistake it prevents (context -> recalled summaries; partnership -> a Q&A interview; interpretation -> researcher assumptions; focus -> a tour of everything). The 'mistake it prevents' column is our framing.
Visual 2: four-principles tile card (see visuals).
Credit: Holtzblatt and Beyer; NN/g (Kim Flaherty, 2020). Write in our own words; do not copy NN/g's or UserTesting's principle definitions.
Disambiguate 'focus' (the focus principle) from a focus group in one clause.

outline.h2: How is contextual inquiry different from user interviews, usability testing and ethnography?
outline.answerHint: Contextual inquiry combines observation and interviewing in the user's real work setting; user interviews rely on recall away from the work, usability testing observes set tasks on your design, and ethnography observes a whole culture over weeks without the focused interview.
points: One sentence introduces the table (table-intro rule). Table rows: setting | what you learn | data type | typical session | sample | best question it answers | main output. Columns: contextual inquiry | user interviews (hub: 10-15 one-hour interviews per user group) | usability testing (hub: 5 participants per round, 1-3 weeks per round) | ethnography. Visual 3 is this table; text version under it.

H3 'What is the difference between contextual inquiry and ethnography?' (PAA): first sentence = direct answer; contextual inquiry is a focused, shorter form of ethnographic field study (NN/g calls it a type of ethnographic field study) with a design question and an interview built in.
The ONE cross-hub link: /services/usability-testing-services/ with anchor 'usability testing services' in the usability testing cell or the sentence after the table.
Use synonym 'contextual research' once. Mention 'focus group' once as the method CI is often confused with in name only (if not used in H2 3).

outline.h2: When should you use contextual inquiry, and when is it the wrong method?
outline.answerHint: Use contextual inquiry early, when the product team does not yet understand how users do complex, expert or physical work in their real work setting. Skip it when the question is about menu labels, a single simple task or numbers across many users.
points: Use when (ul): complex or expert workflows (enterprise software, clinical, logistics), work that depends on the physical environment or other people, a redesign where analytics show drop-off without a reason, a new market whose users work differently (hub 'when to invest' situations; deep link /services/ux-research-services/#when-should-a-product-team-invest-in-ux-research-services is NOT needed; keep links lean).

Wrong method when (ul): information architecture questions (card sorting and tree testing fit better, Maze makes the same point; card sorting is a future cluster post, plain text now), single simple tasks, quantitative questions (survey or analytics), no access to the real setting.
Visual 4: method decision tree (see visuals): 3 questions -> contextual inquiry / user interviews / usability testing / card sorting / survey or analytics. Text version under it.
Future link target (plain text now): the 'ux research methods' pillar post.

outline.h2: How do you run a contextual inquiry session?
outline.answerHint: A contextual inquiry session runs about 2 hours in the user's real work setting and has 4 parts: a short primer, a transition into observation, the contextual interview where you watch and then ask at natural pauses, and a wrap-up where the user corrects your interpretation.
points: Before the visit (ol): research focus in one sentence; recruit 4-6 users per user group (hub figure for our programme; Wikipedia: 4 for a small task to 30 or more); agree site access, recording consent and what may not be filmed (screens with customer data); pair an interviewer with a note-taker.

The session (ol, 4 parts): session primer (introductions, consent, what you will do), transition (from interview mode to 'work as you normally would'), contextual interview (watch, then ask at natural pauses: NN/g's watch-and-learn / stop-and-discuss loop, credit it), wrap-up (play back what you understood; the user corrects it).
Inquiry mode: active (questions during the work) vs passive (questions at the end), credit dscout; when to use each (passive for fast or safety-critical work).

Session length: about 2 hours (Wikipedia, citing Holtzblatt; fact-checker confirms); NN/g says 1 hour to several days by scope. Visual 5: 2-hour session strip with an example time split, labelled 'example plan'.
Observer bias and the complaint-session risk in one sentence each, with the fix (stick to the research focus; ask for the last real instance, not opinions).

Lead moment 1 (end of section): site access, consent and recruiting are the hard part for in-house teams; one natural sentence that our programme schedules recruitment as its own step (hub: participant recruitment 3-6 days). No invented claims.

outline.h2: Which contextual inquiry questions should you ask, and what should you write down?
outline.answerHint: Good contextual inquiry questions point at what the user just did in the real work setting: 'What made you open that second screen?' beats 'How do you usually check orders?'. Write down each step, the tool or artifact used, every workaround and interruption, and the question to ask at the next pause.
points: Question bank as a ul in 4 groups: opening (about their role and today's work), during observation (about the step just seen), probing workarounds and external resources ('Where did that number come from?'), wrap-up (playback). 10-14 questions total, written in our own words; no copying of HubSpot, Nulab or UserTesting lists. Include 3 'avoid' examples (leading, hypothetical, future-preference questions) with the better version.

H3 'A contextual inquiry template for field notes': Visual 6 = field-note sheet (see visuals); its text version is the template table (time | what the user did | tool or artifact | workaround or breakdown | question for the next pause | my interpretation, to check in wrap-up). This covers 'contextual inquiry template' (40/mo). No downloadable file is promised.
Photos and artifacts: collect copies of sticky notes, printouts and spreadsheets only with permission (recording consent).

outline.h2: Contextual inquiry example, a warehouse receiving study
outline.answerHint: This contextual inquiry example follows an illustrative study of warehouse receiving clerks: observation in the real work setting showed a paper packing list, a purchase-order lookup on a second screen and a phone call for every short shipment, none of which came up when the clerks were asked how receiving works.
points: Label the whole example illustrative (composite users, invented details); never imply a client. It reuses the intro clerk so the post has one thread.

Short narrative in 4 beats: research focus ('why does receiving take longer than the system shows?'), 5 sessions at 2 sites (illustrative), 3 observations with the question asked at the pause, and what the wrap-up corrected.
No outcome percentage. End with the 2-3 design questions the observations raised (e.g. show the purchase order on the handheld; a short-shipment flow), which H2 9 turns into decisions.
This is the second stacked H2 ('Contextual inquiry example'); no colon (comma is fine).

outline.h2: How do you turn field notes into design decisions?
outline.answerHint: After contextual inquiry, the team turns field notes from the real work setting into decisions in an interpretation session: 3-8 people replay each session, write one insight per note, group the notes in an affinity diagram, and draw work models that feed personas, journey maps and a Jobs to be Done opportunity map.
points: First sentence must name contextual inquiry (or 'field observation') + one essential concept (see answerHint).

Steps (ol): interpretation session within 48 hours of each visit (our practice; label it) with 3-8 people (Wikipedia/Holtzblatt); one insight per note; affinity diagram across sessions; work models (Contextual Design names flow, sequence, artifact, cultural and physical models; fact-checker confirms the 5 names in the 2nd edition before printing them, else write 'work models such as flow and sequence models'); then the outputs our programme delivers (hub synthesis step: tagged in Dovetail, personas, journey maps and a JTBD opportunity map, 90-minute readout).
No image in this section (6-image cap): the notes-to-decisions path is the ol above, in text. See visualsNote for the optional swap.

Journey map: name it as one output with one sentence; no template content and no steps for building a journey map (the parallel 'customer journey map template' post owns that). Future link target: /blog/customer-journey-map-template/ (plain text until published).

Lead moment 2: synthesis is where in-house studies stall (notes pile up, no one owns the readout); one natural sentence pointing to the hub process step (deep link /services/ux-research-services/#how-does-the-ux-research-process-work, anchor e.g. 'how our 5-step UX research process runs synthesis and the readout').

outline.h2: What does a contextual inquiry study take, and when should you bring in researchers?
outline.answerHint: A contextual inquiry study takes travel to the real work setting, about 2 hours per session plus a few hours of interpretation per session, and 4-6 users per user group. Bring in a research team when you cannot get site access, cannot spare researchers for two weeks of fieldwork, or need the findings turned into personas and journey maps your product team will use.
points: Benefits vs limitations as two short ul (reasoned, not generic): benefits answer PAA (tacit knowledge, real workarounds, credibility with stakeholders, detail surveys cannot give); limitations (resource cost: travel and hours per user, Wikipedia; small sample; access restrictions; observer effect).

Effort numbers in our programme (hub wording only): generative fieldwork 7-15 days inside a 4-8 week programme; on-site contextual inquiry is one of the factors that moves the programme price toward the top of $25,000-$60,000 (deep link /services/ux-research-services/#how-much-does-ux-research-cost, anchor e.g. 'what moves the price of a UX research programme'). State the price once. Do not build a cost section (hub owns 'How much does UX research cost?').

Main lead moment and offer (see leadAngle). Second UP link to /services/ux-research-services/ (anchor varies, e.g. 'our UX research programme'; the exact anchor 'UX research services' is used once early). Sideways link to /blog/choose-ux-research-agency/ (anchor e.g. 'how to compare research agencies before you hire one') for readers who will outsource. Close with /contact/.
Do not use the home.ts MDS-nurses line (CONFLICT 3).

faqs.q: How many participants does a contextual inquiry need?
faqs.hint: Our programme observes 4-6 users per user group (hub). Holtzblatt's guidance via Wikipedia: as few as 4 for a small, focused task, up to 30 or more for a large scope. NN/g frames it as users per visit, visits per day and total visits. 2-3 sentences.

faqs.q: How long does a contextual inquiry session take?
faqs.hint: About 2 hours per user (Wikipedia, Holtzblatt); NN/g: 1 hour to several days depending on scope; remote sessions capped at 2-3 hours (NN/g). Same figure as H2 6 (one intent, one answer).

faqs.q: Can contextual inquiry be done remotely?
faqs.hint: Yes, for screen-based desk work: NN/g calls it 'semicontextual' because only the user is in context; share the entire desktop through screen sharing, keep the researcher camera off during observation, cap sessions at 2-3 hours. It misses physical work, several monitors and in-person interaction. Our programme runs contextual inquiry on-site (hub; CONFLICT 1).

faqs.q: What is the primary objective of contextual inquiry?
faqs.hint: To understand how users actually do their work, including the tacit steps and workarounds they cannot report, so the product team designs for the real workflow. 2 sentences, first is the answer.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of contextual inquiry?
faqs.hint: Short answer listing 4: real behavior instead of recall, tacit knowledge and workarounds, detail tied to real tasks, stakeholder credibility from seeing users at work. Same items as H2 10 benefits, new wording.

faqs.q: Is a contextual interview the same as contextual inquiry?
faqs.hint: Not exactly. In UX research the contextual interview is the central part of a contextual inquiry session (the watch-and-ask loop); many teams use the terms interchangeably. Add one clause that 'contextual interview' also names a clinical interviewing technique, which is unrelated.
